tasks.title: One pass of the event loop
tasks.statement: An AioContext in QEMU does four things: it watches file descriptors, accepts notifications, runs timers and runs deferred calls (bottom halves, BH). In aio_poll(), after the wait, the order is (util/aio-posix.c, QEMU 10.2.0): io_uring completions, then BHs, then the ready fd handlers, then timers. Build a model on the given structures (Loop, Bh, Timer, FdHandler) and implement the functions. loop_init zeroes the loop. loop_add_fd / loop_bh_new / loop_timer_new add a handler and return its index (from zero). loop_bh_schedule(l, bh): if the BH is not scheduled yet, mark it sched and give it the next number ++bh_seq; scheduling an already scheduled BH changes nothing. loop_timer_mod(l, t, expire): arm the timer for the moment expire (armed, number ++tm_seq). loop_timeout(l, now): like aio_compute_timeout, 0 if any BH is scheduled; otherwise -1 if no timer is armed; otherwise the time to the nearest one (0 if it is already due). loop_poll(l, ready, nready, now) performs one pass after the wait and returns 1 if any handler ran, otherwise 0: (1) it takes a slice, all BHs scheduled at the start of the call, clears sched on them and calls them from the last scheduled to the first (this is how async.c reads: insertion at the head of the list; it is not an API guarantee); BHs scheduled during the pass wait for the next call; (2) for each fd in ready, in array order, it calls the handler with that fd (an unknown fd is skipped); (3) while some armed timer has expire <= now, it takes the smallest by (expire, number), clears armed BEFORE the call (as QEMU does) and calls it; a timer armed from a handler for an already due time fires in the same pass. This is a lab MODEL written from scratch (not QEMU code): it repeats the order of actions read in the QEMU 10.2.0 sources, and the model's rules are given in the statement.
tasks.hint: For BHs first copy the indexes and their seq numbers into a local array and clear sched, and only then call them: a handler may schedule a BH again. For timers loop: find the minimum, clear armed, call.

tasks.title: An event notifier on eventfd
tasks.statement: ioeventfd and irqfd in QEMU are EventNotifier wrappers around eventfd (util/event_notifier-posix.c, QEMU 10.2.0). The guest writes to the notify address, KVM bumps the eventfd counter, and an AioContext handler reads it. Implement it on a real eventfd (the sandbox has it). notifier_init(n, active): create eventfd(0, EFD_NONBLOCK | EFD_CLOEXEC), store the fd, set initialized; return 0 or -errno; with active, call notifier_set at once. notifier_set(n): if not initialized, -1; otherwise write 8 bytes with the value 1, retrying on EINTR; EAGAIN is not an error (the counter is full, so the reader will wake anyway); another error is -errno; success is 0. notifier_test_and_clear(n): if not initialized, 0; otherwise read 8 bytes (retrying on EINTR) and return 1 if something was read, else 0 (several kicks merge into one). notifier_cleanup closes the fd and clears initialized. drain_kick(n, handler, opaque) works like virtio_queue_host_notifier_read: if test_and_clear returned 1, call handler(opaque) once and return 1, otherwise 0. A kick made by the handler itself must not be lost. The eventfd is real here, the rest repeats QEMU's logic in our own words.
tasks.hint: Reading a non-blocking eventfd with a zero counter gives -1 with errno EAGAIN: that means no kicks, not an error. Do not loop until empty: one read is enough, it zeroes the counter.

tasks.title: Pop a chain from a virtqueue and give it back
tasks.statement: A split virtqueue consists of a descriptor table, the avail ring (the guest puts chain head numbers there, the counter idx grows) and the used ring (the device returns {id, len}). Below are the ready structures Desc, Avail, Used, Vq and Elem; the indexes avail->idx and used->idx are 16-bit and wrap past 65535. Implement int vq_pop(Vq *vq, Elem *e) after virtqueue_split_pop (hw/virtio/virtio.c, QEMU 10.2.0). The result: 0 means the queue is empty (avail->idx == last_avail_idx, an equality test, not greater/less); 1 means a chain was read; -1 means the ring is broken. The order: (1) empty: return 0; (2) if inuse >= num, return -1; (3) head = avail->ring[last_avail_idx % num], and last_avail_idx is incremented RIGHT AWAY, before the checks; head >= num: return -1; (4) walk the chain from the head: a descriptor with F_WRITE goes to e->in, one without it to e->out, and a readable descriptor after a writable one is an error (-1); if the number of descriptors walked exceeds num it is a loop error (-1); with F_NEXT move to d.next, and d.next >= num is an error; (5) success: e->head = head, inuse++, return 1. vq_push(vq, e, len) gives the chain back: used->ring[used->idx % num] = {e->head, len}, then used->idx++ (16 bits) and inuse--. This is a lab MODEL written from scratch (not QEMU code): it repeats the checks read in hw/virtio/virtio.c and hw/block/virtio-blk.c of QEMU 10.2.0, and the model's rules are given in the statement.
tasks.hint: Compare the indexes for equality and take the ring position modulo num. To check the order it is enough to know whether a writable descriptor was already seen: in_num > 0.

tasks.title: Parse a virtio-blk request
tasks.statement: A virtio-blk request arrives as a chain: the device-readable part (out) starts with a 16-byte header {u32 type, u32 ioprio, u64 sector}, little-endian; the device-writable part (in) ends with one status byte. Read data lies in in (before the status), write data in out (after the header). Guest memory here is the array mem, and a piece is described by Seg {off, len}. Implement three functions after virtio_blk_handle_request and virtio_blk_sect_range_ok (hw/block/virtio-blk.c, QEMU 10.2.0). blk_parse(mem, r, p): return -1 (the device is "broken") if out_num < 1 or in_num < 1; if all out pieces together hold fewer than 16 bytes (the header may be split between pieces, so gather it piece by piece); if the last in piece is shorter than 1 byte. Otherwise fill p and return 0: status_off is the address of the last byte of the last in piece; type is the first 4 bytes; sector is the 8 bytes after ioprio. The kind: type & ~(T_OUT | T_BARRIER) equal to T_IN (0) is a read with T_OUT clear and a write with it set (p->nbytes: for a write the size of out minus 16, for a read the size of in minus 1; sector is taken only for them); T_FLUSH (4) is K_FLUSH; T_GET_ID (8) is K_GET_ID; anything else is K_UNSUPP. blk_range_ok(p, total_sectors): 0 if nbytes is not a multiple of 512, or sector > total_sectors, or nbytes/512 > total_sectors - sector; otherwise 1. blk_set_status(mem, p, status) writes the status byte. This is a lab MODEL written from scratch (not QEMU code): it repeats the checks read in hw/virtio/virtio.c and hw/block/virtio-blk.c of QEMU 10.2.0, and the model's rules are given in the statement.
tasks.hint: Gather the header byte by byte over the out pieces until you have 16 bytes; sizes are sums of len. The status is the last byte of the LAST in piece, not the first.

tasks.title: The vCPU thread loop and the BQL
tasks.statement: In QEMU 10.2.0 the vCPU thread (kvm_vcpu_thread_fn) enters kvm_cpu_exec (accel/kvm/kvm-all.c): the function releases the Big QEMU Lock (bql_unlock) and spins ioctl(KVM_RUN) in a loop while the exit handler returns 0. Repeat the work of chapter 28 with the lock in mind. Implement int vcpu_exec(int vcpufd, struct kvm_run *run). The thread enters with the lock HELD. (1) Call bql_unlock() at once. (2) In a loop call ioctl(vcpufd, KVM_RUN, 0). On error: EINTR or EAGAIN gives RUN_INTERRUPT and leaves the loop; any other error gives RUN_ERROR. (3) Otherwise look at run->exit_reason. KVM_EXIT_IO: the data lies at (uint8_t *)run + run->io.data_offset; call dev_pio(port, ptr, size, direction == KVM_EXIT_IO_OUT) count times, advancing ptr by size; the result is RUN_CONTINUE. KVM_EXIT_MMIO: one call dev_mmio(phys_addr, data, len, is_write), RUN_CONTINUE. These two handlers are called WITHOUT the lock (device code takes it itself when needed). KVM_EXIT_HLT: take the lock, the result is handle_halt(), release the lock. KVM_EXIT_SHUTDOWN: request_reset() and RUN_INTERRUPT. KVM_EXIT_SYSTEM_EVENT by run->system_event.type: SHUTDOWN calls request_shutdown() and gives RUN_INTERRUPT; RESET calls request_reset() and gives RUN_INTERRUPT; CRASH calls guest_panicked() under the lock and gives RUN_CONTINUE; any other type is RUN_ERROR. Any other exit_reason (including KVM_EXIT_INTERNAL_ERROR) is RUN_ERROR. (4) The loop continues while the result is RUN_CONTINUE. (5) After the loop TAKE the lock back (bql_lock); if the result is negative, call vm_stop() (under the lock). The function returns the result. This is a lab MODEL written from scratch (not QEMU code): it repeats the order of actions read in the QEMU 10.2.0 sources, and the model's rules are given in the statement. KVM_RUN is replaced by the model through -Wl,--wrap=ioctl; the constants and the kvm_run structure are the real ones from linux/kvm.h.
tasks.hint: The lock: you enter with it, release it before the loop, take it back after the loop; inside the loop take it only around HLT and CRASH. One iteration's result is a variable ret, the loop is do { ... } while (ret == RUN_CONTINUE).

tasks.title: Coroutines on ucontext
tasks.statement: QEMU's block layer is written as sequential code on coroutines: blk_aio_preadv creates a coroutine (qemu_coroutine_create) and enters it, it submits the request and gives up control (qemu_coroutine_yield), and when the I/O finishes the event loop enters it again. On Linux builds the ucontext backend is the default (QEMU 10.2.0's meson.build prefers it, with sigaltstack as the fallback). Write a simplified version on makecontext/swapcontext. The Coroutine structure is given. co_create(entry, opaque): allocate the structure (calloc) and a stack of CO_STACK bytes, prepare ctx (getcontext, uc_stack, uc_link = &co->caller, makecontext with a function with no arguments); the coroutine does NOT run. co_enter(co): if the coroutine is already running (entered) or has finished (done), return -1 (QEMU calls abort in that case; the model needs a return code); otherwise mark it entered, remember prev = the current coroutine, make co the current one, swapcontext(&co->caller, &co->ctx); when control comes back (a yield or the end), restore prev as current, clear entered and return 0. A coroutine that reaches the end of entry is marked done. co_yield(): outside a coroutine -1; otherwise swapcontext(&co->ctx, &co->caller) and 0 after the resume. co_self() is the current coroutine or NULL; co_done(co) tells whether it has finished; co_free(co) frees the stack and the structure. This is a lab MODEL written from scratch (not QEMU code): it repeats the order of actions read in the QEMU 10.2.0 sources, and the model's rules are given in the statement.
tasks.hint: makecontext takes a function with no arguments, so take entry and opaque from the global current-coroutine variable. The return context co->caller is rewritten on every co_enter and uc_link points to it, so the end of entry returns into co_enter by itself.

tasks.title: Who is who among QEMU's threads
tasks.statement: The command ps -T -p <pid> -o spid,comm prints the threads of a QEMU process. If QEMU was started with -name ...,debug-threads=on, the threads are named like this (by the QEMU 10.2.0 sources): a vCPU under the KVM accelerator is "CPU <n>/KVM" (accel/kvm/kvm-accel-ops.c), an iothread is "IO <id>" (iothread.c), the pool for blocking jobs is "worker" (util/thread-pool.c), RCU is "call_rcu", VNC is "vnc_worker"; the main thread is the one whose SPID equals the process pid. Write a function classify_threads(pid, text): text is the ps output (the first line is the header "SPID COMMAND", which must be skipped; thread names may contain spaces). Return a dictionary with the keys: "main" (the SPID of the main thread, or 0 if it is not in the output), "vcpus" (a list of [number, SPID] pairs, ascending by number), "iothreads" (a list of [id, SPID] pairs, ascending by id as strings), "workers" (how many threads are named worker), "rcu" (how many are call_rcu) and "other" (a sorted list of the names of all the other threads, duplicates included). A thread without a recognised name (for example, because debug-threads is off and every thread is named like the process) goes to "other".
tasks.hint: Split a line into the SPID and the rest: line.split(None, 1). The header drops out because its first field is not a number. Parse the vCPU and iothread names with regular expressions or startswith/endswith.

tasks.title: A disk request's life in a trace-event log
tasks.statement:
Run QEMU with --trace "virtio_blk_*" (the log backend, lines like pid@sec.usec:name arguments, as in docs/devel/tracing.rst) and you get events from hw/block/trace-events and hw/virtio/trace-events of QEMU 10.2.0. For virtio-blk reads and writes the order is: virtio_blk_handle_read or virtio_blk_handle_write (arguments "vdev

req

sector nsectors ") → virtio_blk_rw_complete ("vdev

req

ret ") → virtio_blk_req_complete ("vdev

req

status ", 0 is success). If a request is rejected before submission (for example, a sector beyond the disk), there is no rw_complete: req_complete comes at once with a non-zero status. A flush or get_id request writes no handle events, and its req_complete comes without a pair. After req_complete the request's memory is freed, and the same req address may appear again in a new request. Write a function check_requests(log): skip lines that do not parse as "pid@time:name ..." or whose name is not one of the three events above (including virtio_blk_submit_multireq, virtqueue_pop, noise). The arguments are "key value" pairs separated by spaces. Track requests by the req address and return a dictionary: "ok" is how many requests finished with status 0 after rw_complete; "failed" is the req addresses that finished with a non-zero status, in order of completion; "stuck" is the addresses that had a handle but no req_complete, in order of appearance; "untracked" is how many req_complete events came for addresses with no open handle; "errors" is a list of [line number from 1, kind] pairs for violations: "duplicate_handle" (a handle for an address that is not finished yet; the state does not change), "rw_complete_without_handle" (rw_complete for an address with no open request), "duplicate_rw_complete" (a second rw_complete in a row for one request), "ok_without_rw_complete" (status 0 without rw_complete; such a request is not counted in ok and is closed).
tasks.hint: Keep a dictionary of address → state (handled, rw_done). Parse the pairs as toks = rest.split(); dict(zip(toks[0::2], toks[1::2])). Count line numbers over all lines, the skipped ones included.

tasks.title: Does the guest need an interrupt
tasks.statement: After virtqueue_push the device calls virtio_notify; it decides whether to send the guest an interrupt with virtio_split_should_notify (hw/virtio/virtio.c, QEMU 10.2.0). The logic is this. (1) If the NOTIFY_ON_EMPTY feature is accepted and the queue is idle (no requests in flight and avail is empty), the answer is always yes, and this decision does not touch the state. (2) Otherwise, without EVENT_IDX the answer is yes if bit 1 (VRING_AVAIL_F_NO_INTERRUPT) is NOT set in avail_flags; the state is not touched. (3) Otherwise (with EVENT_IDX): the state is the flag signalled_valid (false at first) and the number signalled_used (0 at first). v = signalled_valid; signalled_valid = true; old = signalled_used; new = used_idx; signalled_used = new; the answer is yes if not v or vring_need_event(used_event, new, old). vring_need_event(event_idx, new_idx, old) from virtio_ring.h is (uint16)(new_idx - event_idx - 1) < (uint16)(new_idx - old), all arithmetic modulo 65536. Write a function notify_decisions(features, avail_flags, start_used_idx, calls): features is a list of strings ("EVENT_IDX", "NOTIFY_ON_EMPTY"), calls is a list of pairs (used_event, idle), one per returned element; before each call used_idx grows by 1 modulo 65536 (starting from start_used_idx), and used_event is what the guest had written into the ring by then. Return a list of True/False, the decision for each call.
tasks.hint: NOTIFY_ON_EMPTY first, then the branch without EVENT_IDX, and only then the state. Compute differences with the mask & 0xFFFF.

tasks.title: Parsing the iothread list
tasks.statement: QEMU's iothread list can be had in two ways. The monitor command info iothreads (hmp_info_iothreads, QEMU 10.2.0) prints a block for each: a line "<id>:", then lines starting with two spaces "  thread_id=<n>", "  poll-max-ns=<n>", "  poll-grow=<n>", "  poll-shrink=<n>", "  aio-max-batch=<n>". The QMP command query-iothreads answers with a JSON object {"return": [{"id": ..., "thread-id": ..., "poll-max-ns": ..., ...}, ...]}; in the example in qapi/misc.json the elements have only id and thread-id. Write a function iothread_table(text): detect the format (text starting with "{" or "[" is JSON; a bare list of elements is acceptable too; otherwise it is monitor output) and return a list of triples [id, thread_id, polling] in order of appearance, where polling is true if poll-max-ns is greater than zero (treat a missing key as 0). Empty or whitespace-only text gives an empty list. In monitor output skip empty lines and the \r character, and also unknown keys and lines without "=".
tasks.hint: json.loads is enough for JSON: the result is a dictionary with the key return, or the list itself. In monitor output a line with no leading space and a trailing colon opens a new block, the other lines are key=value pairs.
